sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Read the verb chains aloud. Keep the stem steady and change only the ending.
items: ich wohne — du wohnst — er wohnt
ich lerne — du lernst — sie lernt
ich arbeite — du arbeitest — er arbeitet
sections.lede: One stem plus six endings is the engine behind most German verbs.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: By the end of this lesson you will be able to conjugate regular verbs and build simple statements.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Most German verbs follow one regular pattern in the present tense. Learn it once and you can use hundreds of verbs.

blocks.text: Take the infinitive, remove the ending -en, and you are left with the stem. Add the personal ending to the stem and you have the present tense. For wohnen the stem is wohn-, so ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt. The present tense covers both “I live” and “I am living”.
Ich wohne in Berlin und lerne Deutsch.
blocks.en: I live in Berlin and am learning German.

items: The endings are -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en for ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie.
wir and sie/Sie use the infinitive form, so they are the easiest to remember.
du and ihr both end in -t or -st, but only du has the s: du wohnst, ihr wohnt.
The verb stays in second position in a statement, even when the sentence starts with a time word: Heute lerne ich Deutsch.

blocks.title: No continuous form
blocks.text: German has no separate “-ing” form in the present. Ich lerne Deutsch can mean “I learn German” or “I am learning German”. Context decides.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The regular endings, plus the small adjustment for stems in -t and -d.

items: If the stem ends in -t or -d, add an extra e before -st and -t: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
The same extra e appears in stems ending in -m or -n after another consonant: du atmest.
A few common verbs change their vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms and must be learned separately: sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; fahren → du fährst, er fährt.
Separable verbs come later; for now, keep the whole verb together.

blocks.title: Word order in three steps
blocks.text: 1) Choose the subject. 2) Put the conjugated verb second. 3) Add the rest. Ich wohne in Berlin. / Am Montag arbeite ich. / Heute lernt sie Deutsch.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: Four regular verbs and two nouns you can use in the same sentences.

items.example: Die Arbeit beginnt um neun Uhr.

sections.title: Example sentences
sections.lede: Notice that the verb never moves from second position in these statements.

items.de: Er arbeitet von Montag bis Freitag.
items.en: He works from Monday to Friday.
items.note: arbeiten adds an extra e: er arbeitet.

items.en: We play football at the weekend.
items.note: wir uses the infinitive form spielen.

items.en: On Monday I do not work.
items.note: The time phrase comes first, so the verb stays second and the subject follows it.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: The endings are quiet. Do not stress them.

items.hint: VOH-nen. German w sounds like English v, and the o is long.
LER-nen. The r is soft and the first e is open, close to “air” without the r.
AR-by-ten. The ei is one glide like “eye”, not two separate vowels.
SHPEE-len. Initial sp is “shp”, and ie is a long ee.
TSIM-mer. German z is “ts”, and the i is short.

blocks.text: Both wohnen and leben can be translated as “to live”, but they are not interchangeable. wohnen refers to where you reside: Ich wohne in Köln. leben is broader and can mean being alive or spending your life somewhere: Ich lebe gern in Deutschland. For an address or a city, wohnen is the safer choice.

When you talk about work, German distinguishes arbeiten (to work) from studieren (to study at a university). A student might say Ich studiere Informatik, while a shop assistant says Ich arbeite im Supermarkt. Both sentences use the same regular present-tense endings.

sections.title: Dialogue in context
sections.lede: A teacher asks her class where they live and work. Listen for the endings.
sections.setting: First lesson of a German course

lines.speaker: Lehrerin
lines.en: Good morning! Where do you live?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.de: Ich wohne in Berlin. Und du, Ben?
lines.en: I live in Berlin. And you, Ben?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.de: Ich arbeite im Café. Ich lerne auch Deutsch.
lines.en: I work in the café. I am also learning German.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.de: Ich arbeite noch nicht. Ich studiere Informatik.
lines.en: I do not work yet. I study computer science.

lines.speaker: Lehrerin
lines.en: Very good! You are learning fast.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: One stem, six endings
sections.lede: The same six endings work for almost every regular verb.

items: Find the stem by removing -en: lernen → lern-, spielen → spiel-.
Add the ending to the stem: lern- + -st = lernst.
For stems in -t or -d, insert e before the ending: arbeit- + -est = arbeitest.
Keep the conjugated verb in second position: Ich lerne heute Deutsch. Heute lerne ich Deutsch.

sections.tip: Cover the right-hand columns of the table and recite the six forms from memory. Speed comes from repetition, not from analysis.

sections.title: Choose the right answer
sections.lede: Choose the form that matches the pronoun.

exercises.explanation: du takes the ending -st: du wohnst.
The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so er takes -et: er arbeitet.
wir uses the infinitive form: wir lernen.
ihr takes the ending -t: ihr spielt.

exercises.prompt: Which form is correct for du + arbeiten?
exercises.explanation: The stem ends in -t, so an extra e appears before -st: du arbeitest.

exercises.prompt: Where does the conjugated verb stand in a German statement?
exercises.explanation: In a main clause the conjugated verb is always in second position.
The ich form ends in -e: ich wohne.
The du form takes -st: du lernst.
Maria = sie, and the stem arbeit- needs the extra e: arbeitet.
wir uses the infinitive form: wir spielen.

sections.title: Build the sentence
sections.lede: Keep the verb in second position, even when a time word comes first.

exercises.explanation: Subject first, then the verb in second position.
sie (she) takes arbeitet, with the extra e before -t.
wir + spielen, then the object Fußball.
Heute is first, so the verb stays second and ich follows it.

sections.title: Listening
sections.lede: Listen to the short interview twice, then answer.
sections.speaker: A journalist and a music teacher

script.speaker: Frau Lang
script.en: Good day. Where do you live?

script.speaker: Herr Ott
script.de: Ich arbeite an einer Schule. Ich unterrichte Musik.
script.en: I work at a school. I teach music.

script.speaker: Frau Lang
script.en: Do you also play music yourself?

questions.explanation: He says: Ich wohne in Leipzig.
He says: Ich arbeite an einer Schule — at a school.
Er sagt: Ich spiele Klavier. Klavier is the piano.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Give a short introduction about your everyday life.
sections.prompt: Say where you live, what you are learning and where you work or study. Use four sentences.

model.de: Ich wohne in Berlin. Ich lerne Deutsch. Ich arbeite in einem Büro. Am Abend spiele ich Tennis.
model.en: I live in Berlin. I am learning German. I work in an office. In the evening I play tennis.

tips: Say the verb and its ending together, as one word: wohn-e, wohn-st, wohn-t.
Start one sentence with a time phrase, such as Am Abend, and keep the verb in second position.
Record yourself and check that every sentence has exactly one conjugated verb.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These errors all involve the ending or the position of the verb.

items.why: The ich form ends in -e, not -en. The -en form belongs to wir and sie.
The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so it needs an extra e before -st.
er/sie/es takes the ending -t: er lernt.
One main clause needs one conjugated verb. Do not add sein to a present-tense verb.

sections.title: Lesson assessment
sections.lede: Ten questions. Score 70% or more to unlock the next lesson.

questions.explanation: The ich form of wohnen is wohne.
er takes -et after the stem arbeit-: er arbeitet.

questions.prompt: What does „Wir spielen am Wochenende Fußball“ mean?
options: We play football at the weekend.
They play football at the weekend.
We watch football at the weekend.
questions.explanation: wir spielen = we play; am Wochenende = at the weekend.
ihr takes the ending -t: ihr wohnt.
The stem arbeit- needs an extra e: sie arbeitet.
wir uses the infinitive form: wir lernen.
The du form ends in -st: du wohnst.
Subject, then the verb in second position, then the object.
The time phrase is first, so the verb comes second and ich follows it.
